newsitem.title: USA: Buffett says its harder to find place to invest.
newsitem.headline: Buffett says its harder to find place to invest.

text.p: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. Chairman Warren Buffett said Monday that as his investment company has grown, it has become more difficult to find places to invest ever larger amounts of money.
"The larger amount of capital we have to work with, the harder the job is," the billionaire investor told shareholders at Berkshire's annual meeting.

"We've had a terrific market that has reappraised all businesses in the last 15 years. We've been aided by a tailwind, but we won't have that tailwind in the future, I can assure you of that. And the larger amount of capital is an anchor," he added.

Buffett said the company has posted gains of 23.8 percent per share compounded annually for the past 32 years in its book value but cautioned that growth would unlikely top 15 percent annually in the future.
"I think 15 percent is absolutely tops," Buffett said. "It could be very substantially lower than that."

Book value is a measure of a company's worth calculated by subtracting its liabilities and intangible assets from its total assets. It is often used by investors as a guide in selecting underpriced stocks.
At the end of 1996, the company's per share book value stood at $19,011.

Buffett, named the world's second-richest man by Forbes magazine last year, answered questions from shareholders for several hours after formally adjourning the business part of the meeting less than 10 minutes after it began.

One shareholder asked Buffett about a comment he made in his latest annual letter to shareholders in which he expressed the opinion that most stocks might currently be overvalued. Had he made this comment, the shareholder asked, in league with Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning about the "irrational exuberance" of the stock market?
"No," Buffett answered. "It's very hard to understand what Alan says sometimes, so it's not much use talking to him.
"My comment was not a market prediction in any sense," Buffett adeded. "We never try to predict the market."
Berkshire Hathaway's share price has long been one of the loftiest on Wall Street, trading Monday at $39,000, up $1000.
Last year for the first time the company issued B shares, valued at 1/30th of the A shares. But Buffett said he planned no further steps to reduce the share price.
"We will not be splitting Berkshire's stock," he said. "We do not consider that a pro-shareholder move. If we did, we'd do it".
The Class B shares were trading up $35 at $1,305.

With the steep price of the A shares, Buffett said, "I think we have a more investment-oriented audience in this room today than we might otherwise have. It's a way of enticing certain types of investors and discouraging others."
